examples.knowledge_point: Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
examples.problem: Estimate $\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)$ using a differential of the function $f(x,y) = \sin x + \cos y$ at the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right).$
examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =-1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\pi + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx  -1  \,  \Delta x + 0  \,  \Delta y
$$

Note that 

$$
\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)= f(3,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3,0.2).$

Moving from $(\pi, 0)$ to $(3,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3-\pi ≈-0.141, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈-1(-0.141)+0(0.2) \\  & ≈0.141.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,0.2) & ≈f(\pi ,0)+0.141 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0.2) & ≈\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0.141 \\  & ≈0+1+0.141 \\  & ≈1.141.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.5-2=-0.5, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+0\cdot (1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ decreases by approximately $0.5.$
